title: Scope of Practice and When to Report Concerns

unit.title: Program Orientation, Professionalism, and Healthcare Roles

sections.learningObjectives:
- Define scope of practice and identify its key sources: state law, employer policy, clinician delegation, supervision, training, and certification.
- Identify clinical and administrative tasks that fall outside the MOA scope and require escalation to licensed staff.
- Describe how and when to report concerns, errors, and near misses, and apply the office's escalation and reporting policy.
- Recognize that medical office assistants perform delegated tasks under licensed supervision and never practice independently.
- Apply "when in doubt, escalate" reasoning to recognize and decline tasks beyond training or authority.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Scope of practice is like the rulebook for a job. It says exactly which jobs you are allowed to do and which ones you must leave to someone else with more training.

### Question 2

The state writes the rules about which medical jobs each kind of worker may do, like how a referee's rulebook decides what players may and may not do in a game.

### Question 3

A certificate is like a badge that says "I learned the skills." But the badge does not give you new superpowers; the rules of the state and the doctor still decide what jobs you may do.

### Question 4

The state's rules are the big rules, like a fence around the yard. The clinic's own rules have to fit inside that fence; they cannot knock the fence down.

### Question 5

Delegation is like a teacher asking a student helper to hand out papers; the helper does the small task, but the teacher stays in charge of the class.

### Question 6

Different states have different rulebooks, just like different schools have different playground rules. The same game may be allowed on one playground and not another.

### Question 7

The doctor is the captain of the ship; the assistant is a helpful crew member who follows the captain's directions and calls out anything unusual.

### Question 8

Administrative jobs are the office side, like being the person who keeps the calendar and the file cabinet organized, not the person who decides about medicine.

### Question 9

Taking vital signs is like reading the thermometer and writing the number down; the nurse or doctor is the one who decides what the number means.

### Question 10

Think of a restaurant: the front desk staff take reservations (administrative), and the kitchen helpers assist the chef with food (clinical). Both help, but in different ways.

### Question 11

Just like different towns can have different rules for dogs on leashes, different states can have different rules for which medical jobs an assistant may do.

### Question 12

Your badge still says you know your stuff, but each new state has its own rulebook, and some rulebooks are stricter than others.

### Question 13

When you are unsure of the rules, read the official rulebook for your job, not the comments section.

### Question 14

An assistant is like a co-pilot: helpful and important, but the pilot is still the one flying the plane.

### Question 15

Learning to use a tool is one thing; being allowed to use it on the job is another. You need both the skill and the permission.

### Question 16

A certificate is like earning a swimming badge; it shows you can swim. A license is like being hired as a lifeguard; it is official permission from the people in charge.

### Question 17

If the school rulebook says one thing but the state law says another, the law wins, and you should tell the teacher (supervisor) about the mix-up.

### Question 18

Scope of practice is like the age rules for driving a car; they make sure only people who are ready and trained do jobs that could hurt someone.

### Question 19

Delegation flows one way, like water downhill: the person with the license hands a small, well-defined job to a trained helper and keeps an eye on it.

### Question 20

Some workers wear two hats: one for the front desk and one for helping the doctor, as long as each hat follows the rules.

### Question 21

The teacher (doctor) stays in charge of the whole classroom, even when the helper (assistant) hands out the papers.

### Question 22

To know if you may do a task, check all four locks on the door: the state's rules, your workplace's rules, your own training, and the doctor's okay.

### Question 23

The BLS "job description" says assistants help keep the calendar and the files in order; the paper-and-planner side of the office.

### Question 24

Assisting is like being the helper who hands the mechanic the right tool; the mechanic still decides how to fix the car.

### Question 25

Reading the number is one thing; explaining what the number means for someone's health is a doctor's job, like reading a map is different from planning the whole trip.

### Question 26

When someone asks a question you are not allowed to answer, the right move is to pass the question to the person who is.

### Question 27

You are not allowed to decide if a medicine should stop; you pass the message to the person who is.

### Question 28

You can take the order and hand it to the chef, but you are not allowed to cook it yourself.

### Question 29

You may help with a tricky task only if three things line up: you know how, the doctor said so, and the rules say it is okay.

### Question 30

Reading an X-ray is like reading a secret code that only trained doctors are allowed to decode; you hand it to the decoder.

### Question 31

No matter how experienced you are, deciding what illness someone has is always the doctor's job.

### Question 32

If someone looks really sick, you run and get the grown-up in charge; you do not guess or send them away.

### Question 33

When you see an unusual number, write it down and tell the person in charge; do not pretend it did not happen.

### Question 34

Escalating is like raising your hand to get the teacher instead of trying to fix the whole problem by yourself.

### Question 35

If you have never learned how to do a job, the safe move is to say "I am not trained for that" and ask the boss for help, not to wing it.

### Question 36

You can run the machine and report the number, but the doctor is the one who explains what the number means.

### Question 37

If a friend asks you whether their tummy ache is serious, the smart thing is to say "let's ask the doctor," not to guess.

### Question 38

Assisting is gathering the ingredients and setting the table; the chef still cooks the meal.

### Question 39

You are not allowed to change the recipe the doctor wrote; you leave it for the doctor to update.

### Question 40

Chest pain is like a fire alarm; you do not decide if it is a real fire, you get help right away.

### Question 41

You can hand someone a brochure, but the doctor is the one who explains the news and what it means.

### Question 42

You may repeat the directions the doctor already gave, like a helper reminding you of the coach's instructions; not invent new directions.

### Question 43

Deciding if someone needs medicine is a doctor's job; the assistant can book the appointment, not prescribe.

### Question 44

If the coach's instruction does not make sense, you ask for it to be explained; you do not just run onto the field confused.

### Question 45

Assisting is being the helper holding the ladder while the person in charge climbs; independent practice is climbing the ladder yourself when you are not the person in charge.

### Question 46

Some jobs are only for specially trained and licensed people, like flying the plane; starting an IV is usually one of them.

### Question 47

The doctor writes the order for tests, like the coach picks the plays; the assistant may help carry it out.

### Question 48

A rash is like a puzzle only the doctor is allowed to solve; you ask the doctor to take a look.

### Question 49

If a note from the boss is smudged and hard to read, you ask the boss what it says; you do not guess.

### Question 50

The law says only doctors may decide what illness someone has, and a workplace rulebook cannot change the law.

### Question 51

If everyone else jumps off a bridge, you still should not jump, especially when the rules say the bridge is off-limits.

### Question 52

In an emergency, you call 911 (or the office's emergency plan) and help if you know first aid; you do not try to be the whole rescue team.

### Question 53

Escalating means telling the right person the important news right away and writing it down.

### Question 54

If the chef is busy, you write down the customer's question so the chef can answer it later; you do not make up an answer.

### Question 55

You do not learn to draw blood by trying it on a real patient for the first time; you get trained first and get the okay.

### Question 56

Questions about mixing medicines go to the experts, the doctor or pharmacist, not to the front desk.

### Question 57

Being supervised means you may do the tasks you were told and trained to do, not make the big decisions yourself.

### Question 58

Signing the doctor's name on a prescription is like signing someone else's name on a check; it is never allowed.

### Question 59

If you write the wrong number on a form, you tell the boss and fix it the right way; you do not scribble it out and hide it.

### Question 60

If you see a teammate doing something dangerous, you tell the coach; you do not look away or join in.

### Question 61

We tell the boss when something goes wrong so nobody gets hurt, like telling a lifeguard when you see someone struggling.

### Question 62

If you see the wrong plate heading to the wrong table, you stop it and tell the person in charge, even if you caught it in time.

### Question 63

If kids are afraid of getting in trouble for spilling juice, they hide it. If they feel safe telling the teacher, the mess gets cleaned up and the floor gets fixed.

### Question 64

If you see smoke, you do not wait until dinner to mention it; you tell someone right away.

### Question 65

If you are not sure whether to tell, it is better to tell; the teacher can decide if it matters.

### Question 66

If a friend tells you someone is hurting them, you get help from an adult in charge; you do not keep it secret or confront the person yourself.

### Question 67

You tell the person in charge at work, not the customers or people outside.

### Question 68

If the first teacher does not listen, you go to the principal; you do not give up.

### Question 69

Write down what actually happened, like a referee's scorecard; just the facts, right away.

### Question 70

If someone falls, you call for help, do not hurt them by pulling them up, and tell the person in charge what happened.

### Question 71

Report what you actually saw, like a good sports announcer calls the play, not who you think is the worst player.

### Question 72

When you are not sure, it is smarter to ask for help than to risk a mistake, like calling a lifeguard when you are unsure if a swimmer is okay.

### Question 73

If someone says "don't tell," but a person could get hurt, the brave and right choice is to tell.

### Question 74

An incident report is like telling the school about a broken playground so it gets fixed before another kid gets hurt.

### Question 75

If a paper lands in the wrong folder, you tell the boss and put it right; you do not secretly shuffle folders and hope it works out.

### Question 76

Just like you do not read a friend's diary to others, you do not share a patient's private details with anyone without permission.

### Question 77

If the microwave sparks, you unplug it and tell an adult; you do not keep using it or poke inside it.

### Question 78

Telling about a safety problem is like telling the teacher about a broken chair; it is not being a tattletale, it is keeping people safe.

### Question 79

After you tell the teacher, you check back to make sure the problem got fixed.

### Question 80

If the bathtub is overflowing, you turn off the water now, not after the floor is ruined.

### Question 81

You should not help hide a spill that someone might slip on; you tell someone so it can be cleaned up.

### Question 82

You tell the people in charge at your own school first, not the whole town.

### Question 83

If you are not sure a job is yours to do, ask the boss before you do it.

### Question 84

Tell the boss exactly what happened, like giving clear directions, not hints and riddles.

### Question 85

If the wrong medicine is given, telling the doctor right away is like catching a spill before it spreads; the sooner, the safer.

### Question 86

You may hand someone their own report card, but the teacher is the one who explains what the grades mean.

### Question 87

The assistant's clinical job is to be a great helper and a good messenger, not the one in charge of the medical decisions.

### Question 88

You can run the heart-photo machine and hand the picture to the doctor; the doctor is the one who reads it.

### Question 89

If your swim badge expired, you tell the coach; you do not pretend it is still valid and jump in the deep end.

### Question 90

If someone says "no," you write it down and tell the doctor; you do not decide for them or ignore their "no."
